findings.claim: The numeric-validity search assumes each loss function is positive exactly when its predicate is violated. If this assumption fails for an operator, the search may optimize the wrong predicate and leave FP exceptional values unresolved.

evidence.support_description: our design assumes that a loss function is positive if and only if its associated predicate is violated by the operator’s input

findings.claim: SparTA's compilation overhead is high for large models, especially transformation and specialization, which limits rapid design-space exploration.
findings.mechanism: Paper reports BERT takes 3 minutes propagation, 2 hours transformation, and 1.5 hours specialization single-threaded -> iterative sparsity exploration requires repeated compilation -> high overhead slows exploration and may be impractical for larger models.
conditions: Large model; single-threaded compilation; repeated exploration.

evidence.support_description: Taking BERT as an example, the propagation, transformation, and specialization take 3 minutes, 2 hours and 1.5 hours respectively using a single thread.
It is possible to reduce the overhead by leveraging more prior knowledge in transformation policy and pre-tuned kernels. We leave it as future work.

findings.claim: WeightedBlockCover uses a greedy heuristic and profiled block weights; for very sparse operators the weights can be inaccurate, and fallback enumeration can blow up combinatorially.
findings.mechanism: Paper uses greedy lowest-cost block cover and profiles block weights -> when operator is too sparse to saturate cores, weights are less accurate -> greedy choice may be suboptimal; enumerating all combinations can be expensive.
conditions: Multiple block sizes; profiling-based weights; very sparse operator.

evidence.support_description: We use a simple greedy algorithm to pick the blocks with the lowest cost

When an operator is too sparse to saturate available cores, the weights may become less accurate. In such cases, we enumerate all the combinations of block sizes to run the weighted block cover algorithm and pick the best one.

findings.claim: Attribute propagation's termination and correctness rely on monotonic, commutative, and associative propagation rules; non-monotonic or context-dependent sparsity rules are outside this guarantee.
findings.mechanism: Paper guarantees termination because each propagation monotonically increases sparsity and rules are commutative/associative -> if a new rule is non-monotonic or order-dependent, the fixed-point algorithm may not terminate or may produce order-dependent results -> extensibility is constrained.
conditions: Propagation rules are monotonic, commutative, and associative.

evidence.support_description: As each propagation monotonically increases sparsity and both the propagations of pruning and quantization are commutative and associative, Algorithm 1 is guaranteed to terminate.

findings.claim: Tensor Scrambling's probabilistic zero detection can misclassify elements when random sampling is insufficient or when zeros arise from operator semantics rather than pruning.
findings.mechanism: Paper treats elements that always stay zero across random scrambles as pruned -> if sampling is too small, a truly nonzero element may never be observed nonzero; if operator produces structural zeros, they may be misread as pruning -> propagation can be wrong.
conditions: Enough random samples; zeros correspond to pruning; operator semantics do not create incidental zeros.

evidence.support_description: treats those elements that always stay zero as pruned elements in an output tensor

findings.claim: The evaluation covers only three models, four sparsity patterns, and three accelerators, so generalization to other model families, operators, and hardware is not established.
findings.mechanism: Paper evaluates BERT, MobileNet, and HuBERT on CUDA GPU, ROCm GPU, and Intel CPU -> these do not cover all DNN workloads or accelerators -> performance and applicability may differ on untested models and hardware.
conditions: Target workload resembles evaluated models and hardware.

evidence.support_description: We extensively evaluate SparTA on three popular DNN models with four representative sparsity patterns on three accelerators

findings.claim: End-to-end results mostly use batch size 32, so latency and memory behavior for other batch sizes is only partially characterized.
findings.mechanism: Paper says batch size 32 except Figure 12 -> batch size affects parallelism, memory, and kernel efficiency -> results may not hold for small or very large batches.
conditions: Deployment batch size differs from 32.

evidence.support_description: The batch size we used in the end-to-end experiments (except Figure 12) is 32.

findings.claim: SparTA does not guarantee accuracy; high sparsity can cause substantial accuracy drops, as shown for MobileNet unstructured sparsity.
findings.mechanism: Paper reports MobileNet unstructured 95% sparsity drops accuracy from 78.27 to 64.15 -> SparTA optimizes latency and memory for a given sparse model -> if the sparsity algorithm's accuracy loss is unacceptable, speedups are not usable.
conditions: High sparsity; accuracy-sensitive application.

evidence.support_description: For MobileNet, unstructured sparsity has a higher accuracy drop, as its sparsity is high (i.e., 95%).

findings.claim: The quantization propagation's acceptable accuracy drop is attributed to knowledge distillation and information bottleneck, but the paper does not fully explain why specific layers can be reduced without loss.
findings.mechanism: Paper uses calibration-based fine-tuning and cites information bottleneck -> it observes 18/28 layers reduce bit width with small accuracy drop -> the causal mechanism for which layers tolerate reduction is not fully characterized -> may not generalize.
conditions: Calibration data and fine-tuning; model similar to MobileNet.

findings.claim: Leveraging Sparse Tensor Cores requires a strict 1x2 sparsity pattern and decomposes the tensor into two sub-Matmuls, so benefit is limited when the pattern does not match.

findings.claim: Execution-plan transformation assumes sub-operators preserve the original computation logic, typically for operators expressible with Einstein summation; arbitrary operators with control flow or side effects are not covered.
findings.mechanism: Paper says sub-operator usually has same computation logic as original, e.g., einsum-expressible -> if an operator cannot be decomposed into such sub-operators, transformation cannot apply -> SparTA must fall back or fail.
conditions: Operator is einsum-like or decomposable with same logic.

evidence.support_description: The sub-operator usually has the same computation logic as the original operator (e.g., the operators that can be expressed with Einstein summation [7])

findings.claim: TeSA stores a two-byte attribute per tensor element during compilation, which can create significant compile-time memory overhead for very large models.
findings.mechanism: Paper says each TeSA element has a two-byte attribute and exists only at compile time -> for models with billions of elements, attribute tensors can be large -> compile memory and traversal cost may become limiting.
conditions: Very large model; many tensors; compile-time memory constrained.

evidence.support_description: Each TeSA element has a two-byte attribute
TeSA exists only during compile time and therefore incurs no runtime memory cost.

findings.claim: Sparsity propagation yields limited gains for unstructured sparsity at moderate sparsity ratios; obvious increases appear mainly at high sparsity.
findings.mechanism: Paper reports propagation ability on unstructured sparsity is lower and only high sparsity brings obvious increase -> for moderate unstructured sparsity, propagation may not expose much additional sparsity -> end-to-end speedup may be smaller.
conditions: Unstructured sparsity; moderate sparsity ratio.

evidence.support_description: The propagation ability on unstructured sparsity is lower. Only high sparsity ratio could bring an obvious increase of sparsity ratio.

findings.claim: Code specialization starts from a dense multi-level-loop implementation generated by a traditional DNN compiler, so operators without such a dense loop implementation cannot be specialized in the same way.
findings.mechanism: Paper says specialization starts from dense version implemented as multi-level loops -> if an operator lacks a dense loop implementation or is an opaque library call -> dismantle and loop specialization cannot be applied -> must use generic kernel.
conditions: Dense loop implementation available from traditional compiler.

evidence.support_description: The specialization process starts from a dense version of the operator, implemented as multi-level loops generated by a traditional DNN compiler

findings.claim: Training acceleration is demonstrated only for NÜWA 3DNA and still relies on PyTorch for some intermediate tensor management, limiting memory and training generality.
findings.mechanism: Paper integrates SparTA-based 3DNA into PyTorch and notes reliance on PyTorch for intermediate tensors -> for other sparse training workloads, integration and memory behavior may differ -> training support is not fully general.
conditions: Sparse training workload; PyTorch integration; intermediate tensor management.

evidence.support_description: As the SparTA-based version currently relies on PyTorch for the management of some intermediate tensor, it is possible to further improve the memory usage by moving it to the SparTA side.
